title: The Houthi threat that Saudi Arabia couldn’t end
gist: Houthi missile and drone strikes on Saudi airports (12+ killed at Riyadh on 10 Oct) and a threatened Bab al-Mandab show that losing Mokha has not ended the Houthi threat to Red Sea shipping, which is the Gulf's remaining oil-export workaround after Iran largely closed Hormuz. Australia, importing ~80% of refined fuel, is exposed and should decide its contribution now.

insights.claim: A Houthi missile and drone strike on Riyadh's King Khalid International Airport on 10 October killed at least 12 and injured more than 300, the deadliest attack in Saudi Arabia in over a decade, and flights in and out of the capital were suspended.
insights.speaker: Isel van Zyl
insights.so_what: Gulf aviation and energy-infrastructure risk premia stay elevated; watch for US joining Saudi strikes.

insights.claim: The Houthis abandoned the 2022 truce in July, declared a maritime blockade of Saudi Arabia, took Mokha and Bab al-Mandab islands in September, then lost both to a government counter-offensive launched 4 October, with the Riyadh strikes as retaliation.
insights.speaker: Isel van Zyl
insights.so_what: The conflict is escalating quickly and back-and-forth territorial swings do not signal de-escalation.
insights.locator: The strike against the airport in Riyadh marks a rapid escalation

insights.claim: US President Trump is weighing whether to join Saudi strikes against the Houthis.
insights.speaker: Isel van Zyl
insights.so_what: A US entry would widen the Red Sea conflict and raise shipping and oil risk.

themes.theme: Red Sea chokepoint and energy workaround

insights.claim: The Bab al-Mandab carries about 30% of global container traffic and 12% of global trade, so Houthi focus on it is deliberate.
insights.speaker: Isel van Zyl
insights.so_what: Any disruption hits container rates and trade flows broadly, not just oil.
insights.locator: The Houthi focus on the strait is no accident

insights.claim: With Iran having largely closed the Strait of Hormuz since US-Israel strikes began in February, Saudi Arabia's Red Sea route (via a newly completed pipeline to Yanbu) is the Gulf's main remaining export workaround, and the Houthis are targeting it by threatening the strait and striking Saudi infrastructure.
insights.speaker: Isel van Zyl
insights.so_what: Concentrated risk on the one bypass route means oil supply security has little redundancy; monitor Yanbu loadings and Red Sea incidents.
insights.locator: The Houthi focus on the strait is no accident

insights.claim: Losing Mokha does not end the shipping threat because the Houthis still hold Hodeidah and their anti-ship missiles and drones do not need to overlook the strait; hitting a handful of vessels would be enough to deter carriers and raise insurance costs.
insights.speaker: Isel van Zyl
insights.so_what: Battlefield gains by the Saudi-backed government should not be read as lower shipping risk; war-risk insurance stays the key indicator.
insights.locator: Losing control of Mokha does not necessarily end that threat to shipping

insights.claim: Iran and its partners now hold sway over both main exits of the western Indian Ocean, Hormuz directly and Bab al-Mandab through the Houthis, while piracy disrupts the waters in between.
insights.speaker: Isel van Zyl
insights.so_what: Maritime energy and trade routes face a compounded geopolitical rather than purely supply-side risk.
insights.quote: This is not just a supply problem; it is a geopolitical crisis.
insights.locator: Taken together, the picture is stark

themes.theme: Horn of Africa spillover and piracy

insights.claim: Since late April six commercial vessels have been hijacked off the Horn of Africa, compared with three in the previous 14 years.
insights.speaker: Isel van Zyl
insights.so_what: A sharp regime change in piracy frequency should feed into shipping insurance and routing costs.
insights.locator: Piracy may be the newest strand

insights.claim: The Houthis are deepening ties with al-Shabaab, trading weapons and training for funding and smuggling routes, and unconfirmed reports suggest they have trained, equipped and even financed some pirate groups as a way to disrupt shipping without provoking the military response missile attacks draw.
insights.speaker: Isel van Zyl
insights.so_what: Deniable proxy disruption is harder to deter, so shipping risk could persist even if missile attacks are suppressed.
insights.locator: The Houthis are extending their reach across the Gulf of Aden

insights.claim: Navies based in Djibouti (US, Chinese, French and Japanese bases) are likely to be cautious about acting against the Houthis for fear of reprisals against their own facilities.
insights.speaker: Isel van Zyl
insights.so_what: Naval protection of Red Sea shipping may be thinner than the number of foreign bases implies.
insights.locator: Across the strait lie Djibouti, Eritrea and Somaliland

insights.claim: Warships can contain the threat at sea but the conditions that sustain it lie on land in Somalia, where al-Shabaab governs large areas, Islamic State is active in Puntland and the African Union mission's future is uncertain after US support was withdrawn.
insights.speaker: Isel van Zyl
insights.so_what: Expect the Horn threat to be persistent rather than a short-lived spike.

insights.claim: Australia imports around 80% of its refined fuel, mostly from Asian refineries running on Middle Eastern crude, while domestic refineries meet only about a fifth of demand.
insights.speaker: Isel van Zyl
insights.so_what: Australian fuel prices and inflation are structurally sensitive to Gulf and Red Sea disruptions.

insights.claim: When Iran closed Hormuz in March, some Australian service stations ran dry and fuel prices rose 32.8% in a single month, and the Reserve Bank has warned those costs are flowing through to other goods and services.
insights.speaker: Isel van Zyl
insights.so_what: Fuel shocks feed second-round inflation, which constrains RBA policy.
insights.locator: When Iran closed Hormuz in March

insights.claim: Australia should decide now on targeted contributions (surveillance, intelligence, staff for counter-piracy and arms interdiction in the Gulf of Aden), build diplomatic capacity on the Horn, and back renewal of the UN weapons-interdiction mandate for Somalia that expires in November.
insights.speaker: Isel van Zyl
insights.so_what: A likely US request for a warship is coming; watch Canberra's response and the November UN mandate vote.
insights.quote: Rather than improvise again, Australia should decide now what it can offer.
